speaker: Matei Zaharia
title: The Agent Cloud: Databricks' Bet on the Future of AI — Matei Zaharia and Reynold Xin
question: In cloud data platforms, why does starting with open-format bulk data processing create a stronger long-term architectural position than starting with a closed, high-speed analytics warehouse?
guest: They started thinking, we will just manage the most valuable data and make it really fast, with our own storage optimized with the engine, starting with the small amount of data that managers and finance people look at. Whereas we started with bulk processing and ingest—large-scale JSON log files and MapReduce-like workloads—and kept the data in an open format. It might be slower at first, but it is already out there to consume downstream. It turned out it is easier to go from that large, low-cost ingest engine and add versions with the speed and features for smaller business-user queries than the other way around. In some sense we started upstream of them. Customers eventually told us, why do I need this other system, why can't I just query your tables? And they realized so much compute was moving upstream. Again, it goes back to enterprises: if your company has existed for thirty years, you have experienced being locked into Oracle and crazy things. When a CTO sets up the architecture for the future, you want an open foundation and ideally one way to manage data, not seven different systems.

points.core: Adding fast SQL serving to a bulk engine beats expanding warehouses upstream.
points.note: Accept: asymmetric expansion where it is technically easier to layer low-latency serving onto a low-cost large-scale ingest engine than to push a curated warehouse into bulk raw processing. Do not credit: generic statements that bulk processing handles more data.

points.core: Compute gravitates upstream to raw ingestion where enterprises store their largest datasets.
points.note: Accept: workloads and processing naturally concentrating at the upstream ingest layer, prompting customers to ask why they need a second downstream system just to query tables. Do not credit: generic claims that data consolidation saves money.

points.core: Long-lived enterprises scarred by past vendor lock-in strongly prefer open storage foundations.
points.note: Accept: decades-old enterprises with legacy lock-in trauma (e.g., Oracle) choosing open file/table formats when setting future data architecture. Do not credit: vague statements that customers like open source.

points.core: Enterprise CTOs want one unified data management architecture instead of seven separate systems.
points.note: Accept: architectural consolidation pressure favoring a single platform spanning ingest, compute, and serving over stitching together multiple specialized data stores. Do not credit: generic claims that simplicity is good.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Starting with open-format bulk processing puts you at the foundation of the data stack, and it is easier to build upward from there than to dig downward from a warehouse.

Data in open formats (Parquet, Delta, Iceberg) on cheap object storage becomes the system of record. All data lands there first, including raw, semi-structured and unstructured data, so the platform owns data gravity. Because storage is decoupled from compute, any engine can read the same files, which lets you add SQL analytics, streaming and machine learning without copying or migrating data. Fast querying is an optimisation layered on later through better engines, caching, indexing and transactional table formats; that is the lakehouse path.

A closed warehouse starts at the top of the stack. It is excellent at fast SQL on structured data, but data must be loaded into a proprietary format that only its engine can read. Extending it to data science, ML or unstructured workloads means either exporting data or re-architecting toward open storage, which undermines its own lock-in and pricing model.

The trade-off is that the warehouse usually delivers better initial performance and simplicity; the open approach wins on optionality, cost and breadth of workloads over time.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Starting with open-format bulk data processing captures upstream data gravity while truly decoupling storage from compute. Because raw, semi-structured, and petabyte-scale data lands first in low-cost object storage using open standards like Parquet and Iceberg, the bulk layer becomes the primary system of record before subsets are ever modeled for business intelligence. Diverse engines for ETL, streaming, and AI training can then read the same files directly without format conversions, data duplication, or SQL bottlenecks.

Crucially, architectural expansion is asymmetric. Adding high-speed SQL analytics onto open tables via vectorized execution, caching, and transactional metadata is an incremental compute upgrade. Conversely, extending a closed warehouse upstream into messy bulk ingestion, multi-modal AI workloads, and external engine interoperability conflicts with its tightly coupled, proprietary storage design—forcing either costly data movement into parallel lakes or a retreat from its closed model. Anchoring on open bulk processing avoids lock-in and pipeline fragmentation, letting specialized compute engines evolve freely over one durable data foundation.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Starting with open-format bulk processing (the Databricks path: Spark over Parquet/Delta/Iceberg in the customer's own object storage) wins long-term because the data stays where it is, in a format nobody owns. Data has gravity. Whoever hosts the system of record for raw, messy, high-volume data (ETL, logs, ML features) sits upstream of everything else. From there, adding warehouse-style SQL performance later is mostly an engineering problem, solved with caching, vectorized engines and table formats with ACID guarantees. Going the other way is much harder. A closed warehouse (Snowflake's original model) is fast and easy to use, but it holds curated data in proprietary storage and charges for compute on it. Moving upstream into cheap bulk processing and ML means persuading customers to pull raw data into a premium silo, and open formats keep that data portable and readable by many engines. That is why Snowflake adopted Iceberg.

The tradeoff is that the closed warehouse often wins early, because it is simpler and faster for BI. As warehouses adopt open table formats, the advantage is shrinking. So this is a strategic thesis, not a settled law.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Starting with open-format bulk data processing establishes a single, vendor-neutral foundation in low-cost cloud object storage using open formats like Parquet or Apache Iceberg. Because storage is decoupled from compute, any engine—whether for batch transformation, streaming, machine learning, or interactive SQL—can read and write the same data without expensive duplication or lock-in. This flexibility is especially valuable as workloads expand beyond structured business intelligence to raw, semi-structured, and AI-driven use cases that proprietary warehouses handle poorly or at prohibitive cost.

More importantly, the architectural evolution is asymmetric. Adding high-speed query engines, caching, or serving layers on top of open bulk storage is straightforward once latency-sensitive analytics needs emerge. In contrast, starting with a closed, high-speed warehouse traps raw data, governance, and pipelines inside proprietary storage and compute models, making it costly and disruptive to later extract data for broader engineering and machine learning workloads.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Starting with bulk processing on open formats gives you a durable data foundation that multiple engines can read. As data volume and history grow, you can reprocess old data, add new workloads, or change compute engines without first exporting and rebuilding the dataset. You can still add a high-speed warehouse later for dashboards and interactive queries, while keeping the underlying data available to other tools.

Starting with a closed warehouse can deliver fast queries sooner. But as more data, transformations, and applications come to depend on its storage and SQL dialect, moving or adding workloads can require large exports and pipeline rewrites. The advantage of starting open is that you can choose where to pay for speed later, without making that first choice a dependency for the whole platform.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Starting with open-format bulk processing puts the most durable part of the platform, its historical data, in a form that multiple engines can read. As workloads change, teams can use the same data for batch jobs, machine learning, or SQL analytics. Where low latency matters, they can add a specialized warehouse and load just the data it needs.

The advantage is the cost of changing direction. Adding fast analytics to an open data foundation can be an incremental decision. If a closed warehouse holds the only authoritative copy, adopting another engine may require exporting years of data, rebuilding pipelines that depend on warehouse-specific features, and keeping copies in sync during the transition. Starting open preserves the option to buy speed where it pays off while keeping future workloads independent of that purchase.
